reading.rtitle: Marketing Brazil -- what the team does
paras: The marketing team in Brazil is small for the size of the operation. Eleven people report to one director, and the director oversees five areas: pricing, trade marketing, market intelligence, brand and communication, and business strategy. He usually starts the day on the dashboard, before the office fills up. He never opens his e-mail first.

The week has a shape. On Monday the team tracks the numbers of the week before and compares them with the target. On Wednesday two people from market intelligence coordinate the report with the sales offices, because the offices often see a price movement before the system does. On Friday the director aligns the plan with the general manager. Once a quarter he presents the whole picture to the board, in English.

The campaigns are the visible part of the job, and they are the smallest part of the week. The team launches something new about four times a year, usually before the rainy season, when workshops buy more. The rest of the time the work is quieter: pricing, share, and the long argument about what a bottle of oil is worth. Market share in this business rarely moves quickly. It moves one workshop at a time.

listenings.text: People ask me what my director actually does all day, and the honest answer is that most of it happens before anybody else arrives. He opens the dashboard first. He never opens his e-mail before that, and he says the e-mail is other people deciding what his morning looks like. On Monday the whole team tracks the week before and compares it with the target, and that meeting never lasts more than thirty minutes. On Wednesday two people from market intelligence coordinate the report with the sales offices, because the offices usually notice a price movement before the system does. On Friday he aligns the plan with the general manager. Once a quarter he presents everything to the board, in English, and everybody in the team notices those weeks, because he asks for the numbers twice.

A weekly number is a very good early warning and a very bad decision. That is the sentence I repeat most often, and people still argue with me about it. A week shows you a direction. It does not show you whether the direction is real, because one week is far too short for that, and half of what you see is weather, holidays or one large customer buying early. The other mistake I see everywhere is the dashboard that grows. A team adds one number, then another, then a number somebody asked for once in a meeting two years ago, and after a while the screen has forty things on it and nobody reads any of them. A good dashboard fits on one screen and answers three questions. And market share, in a slow market, moves slowly. A good team measures it once a quarter, not once a week, and spends the rest of the time on the things it can actually change.
